claim: Cdk1 cKO liver contains less triacylglycerides (TGs) than control liver in 8-week-old mice.
source: The most apparent change in lipid profile from the lipidomics data was that Cdk1 cKO liver contained less TGs than control liver (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), which we separately confirmed with biochemical TG assays (Figure 1B; p=0.0022).
evidence: Supported by lipidomics mass spectrometry data (Figure 1A) and biochemical TG assays (Figure 1B) showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0022).

claim: Control and Cdk1 cKO mice eat the same amount of food.
source: This was despite both control and Cdk1 cKO mice eating the same amount of food (Figure 1C; p=0.6825), implying that this change was not due to a difference in food intake.
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements over 2 weeks showing no significant difference (p=0.6825, Figure 1C).

claim: Cdk1 cKO hepatocyte TG levels are significantly decreased compared to control.
source: We then checked for TG levels in hepatocytes isolated from 8-week-old mice and noted that Cdk1 cKO hepatocyte TG levels were significantly decreased as well (Figure 1D; p=0.0012), illustrating that the reduction in whole liver TG levels were, in part, due to the decrease of TGs in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assays on isolated hepatocytes showing significant decrease (p=0.0012, Figure 1D).

claim: Plasma TG levels are reduced in Cdk1 cKO mice compared to control.
source: Plasma TG (Figure 1E; p=0.0043) and plasma low-density lipoproteins (LDL)/very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) were also reduced (Figure 1F; p=0.0043) with a corresponding increase in high-density lipoproteins (Figure 1G; p=0.0022) in Cdk1 cKO liver compared to control.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assays showing statistically significant reduction in plasma TG (p=0.0043, Figure 1E).

claim: Plasma LDL/VLDL levels are reduced in Cdk1 cKO mice compared to control.
source: Plasma TG (Figure 1E; p=0.0043) and plasma low-density lipoproteins (LDL)/very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) were also reduced (Figure 1F; p=0.0043) with a corresponding increase in high-density lipoproteins (Figure 1G; p=0.0022) in Cdk1 cKO liver compared to control.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assays showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0043, Figure 1F).

claim: Plasma HDL levels are increased in Cdk1 cKO mice compared to control.
source: Plasma TG (Figure 1E; p=0.0043) and plasma low-density lipoproteins (LDL)/very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) were also reduced (Figure 1F; p=0.0043) with a corresponding increase in high-density lipoproteins (Figure 1G; p=0.0022) in Cdk1 cKO liver compared to control.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assays showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0022, Figure 1G).

claim: VLDLs are the main mode of hepatic TG secretion into the blood stream.
source: As VLDLs are the main mode of hepatic TG secretion into the blood stream (Choi and Ginsberg, 2011), this suggested that the reduction in hepatic TGs was not due to an increase in secretion of TGs, but likely a change in TG synthesis or TG breakdown in the liver.
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi and Ginsberg, 2011.

claim: The reduction in hepatic TGs in Cdk1 cKO mice is not due to an increase in secretion of TGs.
source: As VLDLs are the main mode of hepatic TG secretion into the blood stream (Choi and Ginsberg, 2011), this suggested that the reduction in hepatic TGs was not due to an increase in secretion of TGs, but likely a change in TG synthesis or TG breakdown in the liver.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that plasma VLDL levels are reduced (Figure 1F), suggesting decreased secretion rather than increased secretion.

claim: Pnpla2 gene expression is specifically increased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: To address this, we screened a panel of lipogenic and lipolytic genes for changes in gene expression, and interestingly, a specific increase of the lipolytic gene Pnpla2 became evident (Figure 1H; p=0.0022).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0022, Figure 1H).

claim: Pnpla2 encodes the ATGL protein, which is the main rate-limiting enzyme responsible for breaking down TGs.
source: Pnpla2 encodes the ATGL protein, which is the main rate-limiting enzyme responsible for breaking down TGs (Zimmermann et al., 2004), and accordingly, the protein levels of ATGL were increased in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 1I–J; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zimmermann et al., 2004.

claim: ATGL protein levels are increased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Pnpla2 encodes the ATGL protein, which is the main rate-limiting enzyme responsible for breaking down TGs (Zimmermann et al., 2004), and accordingly, the protein levels of ATGL were increased in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 1I–J; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant increase (p<0.0001, Figure 1I-J).

claim: Over-expression of ATGL is sufficient to induce lipolysis in the liver.
source: Over-expression of ATGL is sufficient to induce lipolysis in the liver (Reid et al., 2008), indicating that the reduced levels of hepatic TGs in Cdk1 cKO liver might be due to increased lipolysis mediated by higher levels of Pnpla2/ATGL.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reid et al., 2008.

claim: The reduced levels of hepatic TGs in Cdk1 cKO liver might be due to increased lipolysis mediated by higher levels of Pnpla2/ATGL.
source: Over-expression of ATGL is sufficient to induce lipolysis in the liver (Reid et al., 2008), indicating that the reduced levels of hepatic TGs in Cdk1 cKO liver might be due to increased lipolysis mediated by higher levels of Pnpla2/ATGL.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ATGL is increased (Figure 1I-J) and ATGL overexpression induces lipolysis (Reid et al., 2008).

claim: Cdk1 cKO liver exhibits greater levels of oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, Cdk1 cKO liver exhibited greater levels of oxidative stress, as seen by the induction of antioxidant enzymes Gpx1, Gpx2, Gpx3, and G6pdx (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and the increase in protein carbonylation, which is a good marker of oxidative stress (Dalle-Donne et al., 2003; Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing induction of antioxidant enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and immunoblot showing increased protein carbonylation (Figure 1K), with citation to Dalle-Donne et al., 2003 for carbonylation as oxidative stress marker.

claim: Protein carbonylation is a good marker of oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, Cdk1 cKO liver exhibited greater levels of oxidative stress, as seen by the induction of antioxidant enzymes Gpx1, Gpx2, Gpx3, and G6pdx (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and the increase in protein carbonylation, which is a good marker of oxidative stress (Dalle-Donne et al., 2003; Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalle-Donne et al., 2003.

claim: Foxo1 mRNA levels are increased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Correspondingly, there was an increase of Foxo1 at both the mRNA (Figure 1L; p=0.0079) and protein level (Figure 1M–N; p=0.0065), leading to enhanced localization of FOXO1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) at the promoters of Pnpla2 and Pdk4, a well-established target of FOXO1 (Kwon et al., 2004) (Figure 1O; p=0.0419 for Pnpla2 promoter and p=0.0275 for Pdk4 promoter).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 1L).

claim: FOXO1 protein levels are increased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Correspondingly, there was an increase of Foxo1 at both the mRNA (Figure 1L; p=0.0079) and protein level (Figure 1M–N; p=0.0065), leading to enhanced localization of FOXO1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) at the promoters of Pnpla2 and Pdk4, a well-established target of FOXO1 (Kwon et al., 2004) (Figure 1O; p=0.0419 for Pnpla2 promoter and p=0.0275 for Pdk4 promoter).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0065, Figure 1M-N).

claim: FOXO1 localization at the Pnpla2 promoter is enhanced in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
source: Correspondingly, there was an increase of Foxo1 at both the mRNA (Figure 1L; p=0.0079) and protein level (Figure 1M–N; p=0.0065), leading to enhanced localization of FOXO1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) at the promoters of Pnpla2 and Pdk4, a well-established target of FOXO1 (Kwon et al., 2004) (Figure 1O; p=0.0419 for Pnpla2 promoter and p=0.0275 for Pdk4 promoter).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing statistically significant enrichment at Pnpla2 promoter (p=0.0419, Figure 1O).

claim: FOXO1 localization at the Pdk4 promoter is enhanced in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
source: Correspondingly, there was an increase of Foxo1 at both the mRNA (Figure 1L; p=0.0079) and protein level (Figure 1M–N; p=0.0065), leading to enhanced localization of FOXO1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) at the promoters of Pnpla2 and Pdk4, a well-established target of FOXO1 (Kwon et al., 2004) (Figure 1O; p=0.0419 for Pnpla2 promoter and p=0.0275 for Pdk4 promoter).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing statistically significant enrichment at Pdk4 promoter (p=0.0275, Figure 1O).

claim: Pdk4 is a well-established target of FOXO1.
source: Correspondingly, there was an increase of Foxo1 at both the mRNA (Figure 1L; p=0.0079) and protein level (Figure 1M–N; p=0.0065), leading to enhanced localization of FOXO1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) at the promoters of Pnpla2 and Pdk4, a well-established target of FOXO1 (Kwon et al., 2004) (Figure 1O; p=0.0419 for Pnpla2 promoter and p=0.0275 for Pdk4 promoter).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2004.

claim: Foxq1 mRNA levels show no significant difference between control and Cdk1 cKO liver in young mice.
source: Because FOXO1 transcriptional activity can be repressed by interaction with FOXQ1 (Cui et al., 2016), we determined Foxq1 expression and discovered that there was no significant difference in the mRNA levels of Foxq1 (Figure 1L; p=0.5476).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing no significant difference (p=0.5476, Figure 1L).

claim: FOXO1 transcriptional activity can be repressed by interaction with FOXQ1.
source: Because FOXO1 transcriptional activity can be repressed by interaction with FOXQ1 (Cui et al., 2016), we determined Foxq1 expression and discovered that there was no significant difference in the mRNA levels of Foxq1 (Figure 1L; p=0.5476).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cui et al., 2016.

claim: Feeding Cdk1 cKO mice with NAC reduces protein carbonylation.
source: When we fed Cdk1 cKO mice with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to reduce systemic oxidative stress, we observed a reversal in the amount of protein carbonylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and the mRNA expression of antioxidant enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), Foxo1, and Pnpla2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing reversal of protein carbonylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Feeding Cdk1 cKO mice with NAC reverses the mRNA expression of antioxidant enzymes.
source: When we fed Cdk1 cKO mice with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to reduce systemic oxidative stress, we observed a reversal in the amount of protein carbonylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and the mRNA expression of antioxidant enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), Foxo1, and Pnpla2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing reversal of antioxidant enzyme expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Feeding Cdk1 cKO mice with NAC reverses the mRNA expression of Foxo1 and Pnpla2.
source: When we fed Cdk1 cKO mice with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to reduce systemic oxidative stress, we observed a reversal in the amount of protein carbonylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and the mRNA expression of antioxidant enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), Foxo1, and Pnpla2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing reversal of Foxo1 and Pnpla2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Hepatic TG levels of NAC-fed Cdk1 cKO mice recover to control levels.
source: Furthermore, hepatic TG levels of NAC-fed Cdk1 cKO mice recovered to control levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing recovery of hepatic TG levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: The reduction in hepatic TG levels in Cdk1 cKO liver is in part due to oxidative stress transmitted by the FOXO1-Pnpla2/ATGL axis.
source: This data supports the hypothesis that the reduction in hepatic TG levels in Cdk1 cKO liver was in part due to oxidative stress and this was transmitted by the FOXO1-Pnpla2/ATGL axis.
evidence: Inferred from NAC treatment experiments showing reversal of oxidative stress markers, Foxo1, Pnpla2 expression, and hepatic TG levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E).

claim: Knockdown of Pnpla2 in Cdk1 cKO mice reduces Pnpla2 expression in the liver.
source: Cdk1 cKO mice that were injected with pLKO-shPnpla2 displayed a reduction of Pnpla2 expression in the liver, indicating successful knockdown of Pnpla2.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing reduction of Pnpla2 expression after shRNA injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).

claim: In Cdk1 cKO mice with Pnpla2 knockdown, hepatic TG levels are rescued to levels comparable with control.
source: We then analysed the hepatic TGs in these mice, and found that in Cdk1 cKO mice with Pnpla2 knockdown, hepatic TG levels were rescued to levels comparable with control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing rescue of hepatic TG levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).

claim: There is a negative linear relationship between Pnpla2 mRNA expression and hepatic TG levels.
source: In addition, correlation analysis between relative Pnpla2 mRNA expression and hepatic TG levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) proposed a negative linear relationship with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of −0.84 (p-value<0.0001), supporting the well-established TG lipase activity of ATGL (Zimmermann et al., 2004; Reid et al., 2008) and indicating that the increase of Pnpla2 in the liver of Cdk1 cKO mice is likely causative for the observed reduction of TGs.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing Pearson's correlation coefficient of −0.84 (p<0.0001, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).

claim: The increase of Pnpla2 in the liver of Cdk1 cKO mice is likely causative for the observed reduction of TGs.
source: In addition, correlation analysis between relative Pnpla2 mRNA expression and hepatic TG levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) proposed a negative linear relationship with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of −0.84 (p-value<0.0001), supporting the well-established TG lipase activity of ATGL (Zimmermann et al., 2004; Reid et al., 2008) and indicating that the increase of Pnpla2 in the liver of Cdk1 cKO mice is likely causative for the observed reduction of TGs.
evidence: Inferred from correlation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), Pnpla2 knockdown rescue experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), and citations to ATGL function (Zimmermann et al., 2004; Reid et al., 2008).

claim: All detected AC species are significantly increased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Another prominent observation from our extensive lipidomics data of the Cdk1 cKO liver is that all the detected AC species were significantly increased (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by lipidomics mass spectrometry data (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).

claim: A trend of increase in AC levels is observed in isolated Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
source: This is mirrored by our lipidomic data on hepatocytes isolated from 8-week-old control and Cdk1 cKO mice (Supplementary file 2), which, in all, reliably measured 240 lipid species. Although not statistically significant for most of the species due to the small sample size (n = 3) and large variability, a trend of increase in AC levels in isolated hepatocytes was observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by lipidomics data on isolated hepatocytes (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2), though not statistically significant due to small sample size.

claim: AC is the form by which long-chain fatty acids are transported across the mitochondrial membrane into mitochondria for degradation via β-oxidation.
source: AC is the form by which long-chain fatty acids are transported across the mitochondrial membrane into mitochondria for degradation via β-oxidation (Houten et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Houten et al., 2016.

claim: The accumulation of ACs in Cdk1 cKO liver resembles that seen in patients and mouse models with defective mitochondrial FAO.
source: The accumulation of ACs in Cdk1 cKO liver resembles that seen in patients and mouse models with defective mitochondrial FAO (Houten et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016), implying FAO might be deficient in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Houten et al., 2016 and Lee et al., 2016.

claim: β-hydroxybutyrate levels are decreased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: This was further supported by a decrease in β-hydroxybutyrate (Figure 2C; p=0.0002), a metabolic product of β-oxidation (Grabacka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant decrease (p=0.0002, Figure 2C).

claim: β-hydroxybutyrate is a metabolic product of β-oxidation.
source: This was further supported by a decrease in β-hydroxybutyrate (Figure 2C; p=0.0002), a metabolic product of β-oxidation (Grabacka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grabacka et al., 2016.

claim: Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display reduced basal FAO capacity.
source: When we performed FAO assays on primary hepatocytes from control and Cdk1 cKO mice, we were able to confirm that Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display reduced basal and maximal capacity for performing FAO (Figure 2D–E; p<0.0001 for basal FAO capacity and p=0.0018 for maximal FAO capacity).
evidence: Supported by FAO assay data showing statistically significant reduction (p<0.0001, Figure 2D-E).

claim: Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display reduced maximal FAO capacity.
source: When we performed FAO assays on primary hepatocytes from control and Cdk1 cKO mice, we were able to confirm that Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display reduced basal and maximal capacity for performing FAO (Figure 2D–E; p<0.0001 for basal FAO capacity and p=0.0018 for maximal FAO capacity).
evidence: Supported by FAO assay data showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0018, Figure 2D-E).

claim: None of the FAO genes tested show any difference in transcript levels between control and Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
source: To explore the cause for this, we measured transcript levels of genes involved in mitochondrial β-oxidation. Unexpectedly, none of the genes tested showed any difference between control and Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes, including Ppara (Figure 2F; p=0.1905), the master regulator of FAO (Grabacka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing no significant differences (Figure 2F).

claim: Ppara is the master regulator of FAO.
source: To explore the cause for this, we measured transcript levels of genes involved in mitochondrial β-oxidation. Unexpectedly, none of the genes tested showed any difference between control and Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes, including Ppara (Figure 2F; p=0.1905), the master regulator of FAO (Grabacka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grabacka et al., 2016.

claim: HADHA protein levels are decreased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Interestingly though, immunoblotting for HADHA and ACADVL, two key enzymes in the FAO pathway, revealed a decrease in protein levels of both enzymes (Figure 2G–H; p=0.0286 for both HADHA and ACADVL) despite unchanged transcript levels (Figure 2F; p=0.5476 for Acadvl and p=0.8414 for Hadha).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant decrease (p=0.0286, Figure 2G-H).

claim: ACADVL protein levels are decreased in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Interestingly though, immunoblotting for HADHA and ACADVL, two key enzymes in the FAO pathway, revealed a decrease in protein levels of both enzymes (Figure 2G–H; p=0.0286 for both HADHA and ACADVL) despite unchanged transcript levels (Figure 2F; p=0.5476 for Acadvl and p=0.8414 for Hadha).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant decrease (p=0.0286, Figure 2G-H).

claim: CDK1 modulates mitochondrial import via phosphorylation of the outer membrane protein TOM6.
source: This might be potentially explained by CDK1 modulation of mitochondrial import via phosphorylation of the outer membrane protein TOM6 (Harbauer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harbauer et al., 2014.

claim: In the absence of CDK1, reduced mitochondrial import of FAO enzymes could result in cytoplasmic accumulation that triggers ubiquitin-dependent degradation of these enzymes.
source: In the absence of CDK1, reduced mitochondrial import of FAO enzymes could result in cytoplasmic accumulation that triggers ubiquitin-dependent degradation of these enzymes (Habelhah et al., 2004; Bragoszewski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Habelhah et al., 2004 and Bragoszewski et al., 2013.

claim: CDK1 can enhance fatty acid import into the mitochondria by phosphorylating SIRT3 and augmenting SIRT3-mediated CPT2 dimerization.
source: A more recent finding showed that CDK1 can also enhance fatty acid import into the mitochondria by phosphorylating SIRT3 and augmenting SIRT3-mediated CPT2 dimerization into the functional fatty acid import complex to promote FAO (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: SIRT3 is hypophosphorylated in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Immunoprecipitation of SIRT3 followed by immunoblotting for phosphorylated Ser/Thr affirmed that SIRT3 was hypophosphorylated in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 2I) with no impact on total SIRT3 protein levels (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 2I).

claim: Total SIRT3 protein levels are unchanged in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Immunoprecipitation of SIRT3 followed by immunoblotting for phosphorylated Ser/Thr affirmed that SIRT3 was hypophosphorylated in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 2I) with no impact on total SIRT3 protein levels (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data (Figure 2J).

claim: CPT2 shows increased acetylation in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: In addition, we detected increased acetylated residues upon immunoprecipitation of CPT2 and probing for pan-acetylation (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 2K).

claim: Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display decreased FAO, possibly due to reduced mitochondrial import of FAO enzymes and fatty acids.
source: Taken together, we discovered that Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes display decreased FAO, possibly due to reduced mitochondrial import of FAO enzymes as well as fatty acids that are the substrates of these enzymes.
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced FAO enzyme protein levels (Figure 2G-H), hypophosphorylated SIRT3 (Figure 2I), and increased CPT2 acetylation (Figure 2K), combined with citations to mechanisms (Harbauer et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Many detected FFA species in the plasma are increased in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of plasma samples showed an increase in many detected FFA species in the plasma of Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).

claim: Treatment of Cdk1 cKO mice with NAC does not revert plasma FFA back to control levels.
source: Notably, treatment of Cdk1 cKO mice with NAC, which reversed the hepatic TG phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), did not revert plasma FFA back to control levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), although levels were insignificantly yet visibly lower.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The increase in plasma FFAs is in part dependent on the lipolysis of TGs mediated by ATGL and in part also dependent on impaired FAO in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
source: This would suggest that the increase in plasma FFAs is in part dependent on the lipolysis of TGs mediated by ATGL, and in part also dependent on impaired FAO in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes.
evidence: Inferred from NAC treatment not fully reversing plasma FFA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) despite reversing hepatic TG phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Plasma FFA can be taken up and stored as TGs in white adipose tissue (WAT).
source: As plasma FFA can be taken up and stored as TGs in white adipose tissue (WAT), we investigated whether the increase in plasma FFA resulted in an increase in storage of FFA in the adipose tissue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FFA metabolism.

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice show an overall increase in fat mass.
source: MRI revealed an overall increase in fat mass in Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 3B; p=0.0079), with a higher subcutaneous white adipose tissue (scWAT) weight to body weight ratio and epididymal white adipose tissue (epWAT) weight to body weight ratio (Figure 3C; p<0.0001 for both scWAT and epWAT to body weight ratio).
evidence: Supported by MRI data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 3B).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice have a higher scWAT weight to body weight ratio.
source: MRI revealed an overall increase in fat mass in Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 3B; p=0.0079), with a higher subcutaneous white adipose tissue (scWAT) weight to body weight ratio and epididymal white adipose tissue (epWAT) weight to body weight ratio (Figure 3C; p<0.0001 for both scWAT and epWAT to body weight ratio).
evidence: Supported by tissue weight measurements showing statistically significant increase (p<0.0001, Figure 3C).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice have a higher epWAT weight to body weight ratio.
source: MRI revealed an overall increase in fat mass in Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 3B; p=0.0079), with a higher subcutaneous white adipose tissue (scWAT) weight to body weight ratio and epididymal white adipose tissue (epWAT) weight to body weight ratio (Figure 3C; p<0.0001 for both scWAT and epWAT to body weight ratio).
evidence: Supported by tissue weight measurements showing statistically significant increase (p<0.0001, Figure 3C).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice show a more pronounced increase in body weight compared to control mice.
source: This might, in part, explain the more pronounced increase in body weight of Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 3D–E) despite the similar food intake between both groups of mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements (Figure 3D-E).

claim: Adipocytes in scWAT are significantly increased in size in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Histological staining of the scWAT and epWAT (Figure 3F) indicated that adipocytes were significantly increased in size, from 494 (±49)μm2 in control scWAT to 692 (±63)μm2 in Cdk1 cKO scWAT and 589 (±86)μm2 in control epWAT to 1066 (±153)μm2 in Cdk1 cKO epWAT (Figure 3G; p=0.0079 for both scWAT and epWAT).
evidence: Supported by histological quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 3F-G).

claim: Adipocytes in epWAT are significantly increased in size in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Histological staining of the scWAT and epWAT (Figure 3F) indicated that adipocytes were significantly increased in size, from 494 (±49)μm2 in control scWAT to 692 (±63)μm2 in Cdk1 cKO scWAT and 589 (±86)μm2 in control epWAT to 1066 (±153)μm2 in Cdk1 cKO epWAT (Figure 3G; p=0.0079 for both scWAT and epWAT).
evidence: Supported by histological quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 3F-G).

claim: Cdk1 cKO WAT contains higher levels of TGs.
source: Biochemical assays further confirmed that Cdk1 cKO WAT contained higher levels of TGs (Figure 3H; p=0.0079 for both scWAT and epWAT).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 3H).

claim: Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 are decreased in Cdk1 cKO WAT.
source: When we then probed Cdk1 cKO WAT for the expression of genes involved with fatty acid synthesis, we found that Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 were decreased (Figure 3I–J), implying that the increase in TGs was not due to increases in WAT fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 3I-J).

claim: The increase in TGs in Cdk1 cKO WAT is not due to increases in WAT fatty acid synthesis.
source: When we then probed Cdk1 cKO WAT for the expression of genes involved with fatty acid synthesis, we found that Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 were decreased (Figure 3I–J), implying that the increase in TGs was not due to increases in WAT fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from decreased expression of lipogenic genes (Figure 3I-J).

claim: Repression of de novo lipogenesis in WAT parallels what is seen in mice fed with high fat diet.
source: Instead, this repression of de novo lipogenesis parallels what is seen in mice fed with high fat diet, whereby there is elevated supply of dietary fat to the WAT via the blood stream (Shillabeer et al., 1990; Tovar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shillabeer et al., 1990 and Tovar et al., 2011.

claim: The increase of plasma FFA leads to elevated storage of FFA as TGs in WAT of Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: These results thus suggest that the increase of plasma FFA led to elevated storage of FFA as TGs in WAT of Cdk1 cKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from increased plasma FFA (Figure 3A), increased WAT TG (Figure 3H), and decreased lipogenic gene expression in WAT (Figure 3I-J).

claim: Expression of FAO-associated genes in skeletal muscle is increased in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: For example, the expression of FAO enzymes in the skeletal muscle are boosted in the presence of elevated plasma FFA levels (Garcia-Roves et al., 2007). In accordance with this, we observed increased expression of various FAO-associated genes in the skeletal muscle of Cdk1 cKO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 4A) and citation to Garcia-Roves et al., 2007.

claim: Plasma FFAs promote insulin secretion by pancreatic β-cells even in the fasting state.
source: Of particular interest is the fact that plasma FFAs are also known to promote insulin secretion by pancreatic β-cells even in the fasting state (Itoh et al., 2003; Cen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Itoh et al., 2003 and Cen et al., 2016.

claim: Plasma insulin is increased in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, we detected increased plasma insulin in Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 4B; p=0.0499), a state known as hyperinsulinemia, despite there being no difference in the transcript level of Ins2 between Cdk1 cKO and control pancreas (Figure 4C; p=0.8413).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0499, Figure 4B).

claim: There is no difference in Ins2 transcript levels between Cdk1 cKO and control pancreas.
source: Interestingly, we detected increased plasma insulin in Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 4B; p=0.0499), a state known as hyperinsulinemia, despite there being no difference in the transcript level of Ins2 between Cdk1 cKO and control pancreas (Figure 4C; p=0.8413).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing no significant difference (p=0.8413, Figure 4C).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice display reduced blood glucose levels.
source: Furthermore, Cdk1 cKO mice displayed reduced blood glucose levels (Figure 4D; p<0.0001) and greater hepatic glycogen content (Figure 4E; p=0.0079), both of which are phenotypes associated with enhanced insulin signaling.
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements showing statistically significant reduction (p<0.0001, Figure 4D).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice display greater hepatic glycogen content.
source: Furthermore, Cdk1 cKO mice displayed reduced blood glucose levels (Figure 4D; p<0.0001) and greater hepatic glycogen content (Figure 4E; p=0.0079), both of which are phenotypes associated with enhanced insulin signaling.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 4E).

claim: Enhanced phosphorylation of INSRB is observed in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: This was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 4F), where we observed enhanced phosphorylation of INSRB (Figure 4G; p=0.0312) and AKT (Figure 4H; p=0.0042) in Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0312, Figure 4F-G).

claim: Enhanced phosphorylation of AKT is observed in Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: This was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 4F), where we observed enhanced phosphorylation of INSRB (Figure 4G; p=0.0312) and AKT (Figure 4H; p=0.0042) in Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0042, Figure 4F, 4H).

claim: Cdk1 cKO mice are more glucose tolerant and respond better to exogenous glucose.
source: When we performed glucose tolerance tests (Figure 4I), Cdk1 cKO mice were more glucose tolerant and responded better to exogenous glucose, as seen from a lower area under the curve (Figure 4J; p<0.0001), which is likely a result of the increased insulin levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data showing statistically significant lower area under curve (p<0.0001, Figure 4I-J).

claim: The elevated plasma FFA promotes insulin secretion and maintains a hyperinsulinemic condition in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that the elevated plasma FFA promotes insulin secretion and maintains a hyperinsulinemic condition in Cdk1 cKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from elevated plasma FFA (Figure 3A), increased plasma insulin (Figure 4B), and established knowledge that FFAs promote insulin secretion (Itoh et al., 2003; Cen et al., 2016).

claim: Chronic hyperinsulinemia can lead to insulin resistance in patients.
source: Chronic hyperinsulinemia can lead to insulin resistance in patients (Morita et al., 2017), hence we wondered whether plasma insulin remained high in Cdk1 cKO mice over time.
evidence: Supported by citation to Morita et al., 2017.

claim: Plasma insulin remains elevated in Cdk1 cKO mice at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: We analyzed plasma insulin levels of 6- and 12-month-old mice and found that plasma insulin was increased from an average of 0.6 ng/mL in control mice to 1.4 ng/mL in Cdk1 cKO mice at 6 months old and from an average of 1 ng/mL in control mice to 2 ng/mL in Cdk1 cKO mice at 12 months old (Figure 5A; p=0.0079 for both 6 and 12 months).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing statistically significant increases at both time points (p=0.0079, Figure 5A).

claim: Plasma FFAs remain consistently higher in Cdk1 cKO mice at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: This paralleled the consistently higher levels of plasma FFAs in Cdk1 cKO mice compared to age-matched control mice at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5B; p=0.0079 for both 6 and 12 months).
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant increases at both time points (p=0.0079, Figure 5B).

claim: Total INSRB protein levels are reduced in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: When we checked for insulin signaling in the aged liver by immunoblotting (Figure 5C), we noticed the levels of total INSRB protein was reduced (Figure 5D; p=0.0220), which might be due to chronic exposure to hyperinsulinemia (Ronnett et al., 1982; Palsgaard et al., 2009) that can, in part, lead to insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0220, Figure 5C-D).

claim: Chronic exposure to hyperinsulinemia can lead to reduced INSRB protein levels.
source: When we checked for insulin signaling in the aged liver by immunoblotting (Figure 5C), we noticed the levels of total INSRB protein was reduced (Figure 5D; p=0.0220), which might be due to chronic exposure to hyperinsulinemia (Ronnett et al., 1982; Palsgaard et al., 2009) that can, in part, lead to insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ronnett et al., 1982 and Palsgaard et al., 2009.

claim: INSRB phosphorylation is reduced in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: We also detected hypophosphorylated INSRB, even after normalizing to total INSRB levels (Figure 5E; p=0.0289), and hypophosphorylated AKT (Figure 5F; p=0.0191), suggesting that insulin signaling was impaired in the liver despite higher plasma insulin levels.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0289, Figure 5C, 5E).

claim: AKT phosphorylation is reduced in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: We also detected hypophosphorylated INSRB, even after normalizing to total INSRB levels (Figure 5E; p=0.0289), and hypophosphorylated AKT (Figure 5F; p=0.0191), suggesting that insulin signaling was impaired in the liver despite higher plasma insulin levels.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0191, Figure 5C, 5F).

claim: Insulin signaling is impaired in aged Cdk1 cKO liver despite higher plasma insulin levels.
source: We also detected hypophosphorylated INSRB, even after normalizing to total INSRB levels (Figure 5E; p=0.0289), and hypophosphorylated AKT (Figure 5F; p=0.0191), suggesting that insulin signaling was impaired in the liver despite higher plasma insulin levels.
evidence: Inferred from reduced INSRB and AKT phosphorylation (Figure 5E-F) despite elevated plasma insulin (Figure 5A).

claim: Insulin signaling is defective in adipose tissues of aged Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: A similar observation was made from immunoblots of epWAT collected from aged Cdk1 cKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), whereby we noted decreased INSRB protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; p=0.0253) and hypophosphorylated INSRB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; p<0.0001) and AKT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; p=0.0034), hinting at defective insulin signaling in adipose tissues as well.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from epWAT showing reduced INSRB protein and phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: Adiponectin (Adipoq) expression is diminished in aged Cdk1 cKO epWAT.
source: This was supported by the change in expression of a number of adipokines in the epWAT. In particular, adiponectin (Adipoq) expression was diminished and resistin (Retn) expression was increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), both of which are associated with insulin resistance (Kadowaki, 2006; Jiang et al., 2016), especially since adiponectin represses the expression of gluconeogenic genes in hepatocytes and promotes membrane localization of GLUT4 in myocytes to increase the uptake of glucose (Combs et al., 2001; Yamauchi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Resistin (Retn) expression is increased in aged Cdk1 cKO epWAT.
source: This was supported by the change in expression of a number of adipokines in the epWAT. In particular, adiponectin (Adipoq) expression was diminished and resistin (Retn) expression was increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), both of which are associated with insulin resistance (Kadowaki, 2006; Jiang et al., 2016), especially since adiponectin represses the expression of gluconeogenic genes in hepatocytes and promotes membrane localization of GLUT4 in myocytes to increase the uptake of glucose (Combs et al., 2001; Yamauchi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Diminished adiponectin and increased resistin expression are associated with insulin resistance.
source: This was supported by the change in expression of a number of adipokines in the epWAT. In particular, adiponectin (Adipoq) expression was diminished and resistin (Retn) expression was increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), both of which are associated with insulin resistance (Kadowaki, 2006; Jiang et al., 2016), especially since adiponectin represses the expression of gluconeogenic genes in hepatocytes and promotes membrane localization of GLUT4 in myocytes to increase the uptake of glucose (Combs et al., 2001; Yamauchi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kadowaki, 2006; Jiang et al., 2016; Combs et al., 2001; Yamauchi et al., 2002.

claim: Fgf21 and Gdf15 expression is increased in aged Cdk1 cKO epWAT.
source: We also observed an increase in expression of Fgf21 and Gdf15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), which reflects the state of metabolic stress that the mice are in Manoli et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2019.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and citations to Manoli et al., 2018 and Patel et al., 2019.

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice display increased blood glucose levels.
source: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice displayed increased blood glucose levels (Figure 5G; p<0.0001) and reduced hepatic glycogen content (Figure 5H; p=0.0079), indicating that 12-month-old Cdk1 cKO mice had developed insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements showing statistically significant increase (p<0.0001, Figure 5G).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice display reduced hepatic glycogen content.
source: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice displayed increased blood glucose levels (Figure 5G; p<0.0001) and reduced hepatic glycogen content (Figure 5H; p=0.0079), indicating that 12-month-old Cdk1 cKO mice had developed insulin resistance.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant reduction (p=0.0079, Figure 5H).

claim: 12-month-old Cdk1 cKO mice have developed insulin resistance.
source: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice displayed increased blood glucose levels (Figure 5G; p<0.0001) and reduced hepatic glycogen content (Figure 5H; p=0.0079), indicating that 12-month-old Cdk1 cKO mice had developed insulin resistance.
evidence: Inferred from increased blood glucose (Figure 5G), reduced hepatic glycogen (Figure 5H), impaired insulin signaling (Figure 5C-F), and glucose/insulin tolerance tests (Figure 5I-L).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice are more glucose intolerant than control mice.
source: When we performed glucose and insulin tolerance tests in 12-month-old mice, Cdk1 cKO mice were more glucose intolerant (Figure 5I–J; p=0.0057) and less insulin sensitive (Figure 5K–L; p=0.0079) than control mice.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data showing statistically significant higher area under curve (p=0.0057, Figure 5I-J).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice are less insulin sensitive than control mice.
source: When we performed glucose and insulin tolerance tests in 12-month-old mice, Cdk1 cKO mice were more glucose intolerant (Figure 5I–J; p=0.0057) and less insulin sensitive (Figure 5K–L; p=0.0079) than control mice.
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data showing statistically significant lower area above curve (p=0.0079, Figure 5K-L).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice develop insulin resistance, possibly due to chronic hyperinsulinemia.
source: Taken together, aged Cdk1 cKO mice develop insulin resistance, possibly due to chronic hyperinsulinemia.
evidence: Inferred from sustained hyperinsulinemia (Figure 5A), impaired insulin signaling (Figure 5C-F), and glucose/insulin tolerance tests (Figure 5I-L), combined with knowledge that chronic hyperinsulinemia causes insulin resistance (Morita et al., 2017).

claim: Hepatic steatosis is present in up to 50% of patients with type 2 diabetes.
source: Hepatic steatosis is present in up to 50% of patients with type 2 diabetes (Roden, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roden, 2006.

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice exhibit macrovesicular fatty changes in the liver.
source: Histopathological analysis of hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained liver sections from 12-month-old mice by a certified pathologist revealed the presence of macrovesicular fatty changes in aged Cdk1 cKO mice, with control mice scoring 0, indicating the lack of any observable fatty changes, while Cdk1 cKO mice were more variable with an average score of 1.8, but with some scoring as high as 4 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis data (Supplementary file 4).

claim: Lipid droplets are present in most aged Cdk1 cKO mice but not in any of the aged control mice.
source: This was confirmed by Oil Red O staining that illustrated the presence of lipid droplets in most aged Cdk1 cKO mice but not in any of the aged control mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by Oil Red O staining images (Figure 6A).

claim: Hepatic TG levels are higher in aged Cdk1 cKO liver relative to control.
source: Additionally, TG assays (Figure 6B; p=0.0079) confirmed higher levels of hepatic TG in Cdk1 cKO liver relative to control.
evidence: Supported by biochemical assay data showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0079, Figure 6B).

claim: Expression of Acaca, Fasn, Mogat1, and Cidec is greater in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: There was also greater expression of Acaca, Fasn, Mogat1, and Cidec (Figure 6C), which are genes associated with lipogenesis and lipid accumulation, as well as increased protein level of the lipogenic transcription factor SREBP1c (Figure 6D–E; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 6C).

claim: SREBP1c protein levels are increased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: There was also greater expression of Acaca, Fasn, Mogat1, and Cidec (Figure 6C), which are genes associated with lipogenesis and lipid accumulation, as well as increased protein level of the lipogenic transcription factor SREBP1c (Figure 6D–E; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot quantification showing statistically significant increase (p<0.0001, Figure 6D-E).

claim: Nearly all of the 180 TG species detected are elevated in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Even at 12 months old, lipidomics analysis (390 species detected) indicated that there were elevated levels of nearly all the 180 TG species detected (Figure 6F, Supplementary file 5), which could be correlated to the presence of insulin resistance (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by lipidomics data (Figure 6F, Supplementary file 5).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice develop hepatic steatosis, possibly through the upregulation of the lipogenic pathway.
source: Hence, we present convincing data that aged Cdk1 cKO mice develop hepatic steatosis, possibly through the upregulation of the lipogenic pathway but the mechanisms for this need to be further investigated (see below).
evidence: Inferred from histological evidence of steatosis (Figure 6A), increased hepatic TG (Figure 6B), increased lipogenic gene expression (Figure 6C), and increased SREBP1c (Figure 6D-E).

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO mice exhibit more fibrotic areas compared to control.
source: About 20% of patients with NAFLD progress to NASH, characterized by the development of fibrosis (Farrell and Larter, 2006). Therefore, we also probed whether aged Cdk1 cKO mice develop liver fibrosis. Sirius Red staining indicated that aged Cdk1 cKO mice exhibited more fibrotic areas compared to control (Figure 6G; p=0.0043), with some mice developing parenchymal and bridging fibrosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by Sirius Red staining quantification showing statistically significant increase (p=0.0043, Figure 6A, 6G).

claim: About 20% of patients with NAFLD progress to NASH, characterized by the development of fibrosis.
source: About 20% of patients with NAFLD progress to NASH, characterized by the development of fibrosis (Farrell and Larter, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrell and Larter, 2006.

claim: Hepatocyte ballooning is present in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Coupled to the presence of hepatocyte ballooning in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6A), another histological feature of NASH (Lackner, 2011), our histological data supports the progression to a NASH-like state in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Supported by histological images (Figure 6A).

claim: Hepatocyte ballooning is a histological feature of NASH.
source: Coupled to the presence of hepatocyte ballooning in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6A), another histological feature of NASH (Lackner, 2011), our histological data supports the progression to a NASH-like state in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lackner, 2011.

claim: Aged Cdk1 cKO liver progresses to a NASH-like state.
source: Coupled to the presence of hepatocyte ballooning in Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6A), another histological feature of NASH (Lackner, 2011), our histological data supports the progression to a NASH-like state in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Inferred from presence of steatosis (Figure 6A-B), fibrosis (Figure 6A, 6G), and hepatocyte ballooning (Figure 6A).

claim: TGs and diacylglycerides are increased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver according to metabolomics data.
source: There was a substantial amount of lipids identified in the metabolomics data, likely due to the method of metabolite extraction used (Narayanaswamy et al., 2020). Nevertheless, in line with our lipidomics data (Figure 6F) and histological observations (Figure 6A), TGs were increased in Cdk1 cKO liver, as were diacylglycerides (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6H) from Narayanaswamy et al., 2020.

claim: Most detected AC species are increased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: We also found that most detected AC species were increased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6I), similar to what was seen in 8-week-old Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 2A–B), which might imply that the loss of FAO in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes (Figure 2C–E) was sustained in aging.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6I).

claim: The loss of FAO in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes is sustained in aging.
source: We also found that most detected AC species were increased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6I), similar to what was seen in 8-week-old Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 2A–B), which might imply that the loss of FAO in Cdk1 cKO hepatocytes (Figure 2C–E) was sustained in aging.
evidence: Inferred from persistent elevation of ACs in both young (Figure 2A-B) and aged (Figure 6I) Cdk1 cKO liver.

claim: Acetylcarnitine is reduced in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Acetylcarnitine, a subspecies of ACs, was the only AC species reduced and among the most diminished metabolites in aged Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6I).

claim: The reduction of acetylcarnitine could be due to the diversion of acetyl-CoA toward the lipogenic pathway.
source: This could be due to the diversion of acetyl-CoA toward the lipogenic pathway (Figure 6C–E), thereby reducing the need for carnitine to buffer acetyl-CoA levels in cells.
evidence: Inferred from increased lipogenic gene expression (Figure 6C) and SREBP1c levels (Figure 6D-E).

claim: Retinol and retinal are the most decreased metabolites in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Other notable metabolites that were changed in aged Cdk1 cKO liver compared to control include retinol and retinal (Figure 6J), which were the most decreased metabolites observed in the metabolomics data, and both oxidized and reduced forms of glutathione (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6J).

claim: Decreases of hepatic retinol and retinal might be an outcome of hepatic stellate cell activation.
source: Decreases of hepatic retinol and retinal (Figure 6J) might be an outcome of hepatic stellate cell activation, as evidenced by the increased fibrosis (Figure 6A), and the resultant loss of lipid droplets in these cells, which are the main stores of retinoids in the liver (Narayanaswamy et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from decreased retinol/retinal (Figure 6J), increased fibrosis (Figure 6A), and citation to Narayanaswamy et al., 2020.

claim: Oxidized glutathione is increased and reduced glutathione is decreased in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Other notable metabolites that were changed in aged Cdk1 cKO liver compared to control include retinol and retinal (Figure 6J), which were the most decreased metabolites observed in the metabolomics data, and both oxidized and reduced forms of glutathione (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6K).

claim: The increase of oxidized glutathione and decrease of reduced glutathione reflect the altered redox status in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: The increase of oxidized glutathione and decrease of reduced glutathione could reflect the altered redox status in Cdk1 cKO liver that was evident even in young mice (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from glutathione redox changes (Figure 6K) and oxidative stress observed in young mice (Figure 1).

claim: Inosine, guanosine, xanthosine, and urate are elevated in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Interestingly, metabolites from the purine metabolism pathway, namely inosine, guanosine, xanthosine, and urate, were elevated (Figure 6L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 6L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is more active in type 2 diabetic patients.
source: This is particularly intriguing because adenosine deaminase (ADA), the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of adenosine to inosine, is known to be more active in type 2 diabetic patients (Kurtul et al., 2004) and is associated with liver fibrosis in NAFLD (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurtul et al., 2004.

claim: ADA is associated with liver fibrosis in NAFLD.
source: This is particularly intriguing because adenosine deaminase (ADA), the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of adenosine to inosine, is known to be more active in type 2 diabetic patients (Kurtul et al., 2004) and is associated with liver fibrosis in NAFLD (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2018.

claim: Elevated serum urate level is a biomarker and risk factor for fatty liver disease.
source: In fact, the presence of elevated serum urate level is a biomarker and risk factor for fatty liver disease (Jensen et al., 2018), and greater XDH activity has been suggested as a causative factor for the development of insulin resistance and NAFLD through increasing oxidative stress via production of hydrogen peroxide (Kelley et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2018.

claim: Greater XDH activity has been suggested as a causative factor for the development of insulin resistance and NAFLD through increasing oxidative stress.
source: In fact, the presence of elevated serum urate level is a biomarker and risk factor for fatty liver disease (Jensen et al., 2018), and greater XDH activity has been suggested as a causative factor for the development of insulin resistance and NAFLD through increasing oxidative stress via production of hydrogen peroxide (Kelley et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kelley et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Control and Cdk1 cKO samples cluster separately along the PC1 axis in principal component analysis of transcriptomic data.
source: Principal component analysis of the transcriptomic data indicated that control and Cdk1 cKO samples clustered separately along the PC1 axis, with the PC1 axis accounting for 68.7% of the variability among the samples, and that the transcriptomes of aged control samples were more similar to each other while those of Cdk1 cKO liver were more heterogeneous (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis of RNA-seq data (Figure 7A).

claim: 310 genes are upregulated and 72 genes are downregulated in aged Cdk1 cKO liver relative to control.
source: We identified a total of 12,143 genes, including 310 genes that were upregulated and 72 that were downregulated in Cdk1 cKO liver relative to control (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 6).

claim: Gsta1 is one of the most differentially expressed genes between normal liver and steatotic liver.
source: Some of the top upregulated were predicted genes with relatively unknown functions, such as Gm14295, Gm11007, and Gm2007, although we also found genes such as Gsta1, an oxidative stress response gene that is one of the most differentially expressed between normal liver and steatotic liver (Hennig et al., 2014), and retinol metabolism genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b13, and Rdh9, which is part of a predictive signature for fibrosis in a mouse model for NASH (van Koppen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hennig et al., 2014.

claim: Rdh9 is part of a predictive signature for fibrosis in a mouse model for NASH.
source: Some of the top upregulated were predicted genes with relatively unknown functions, such as Gm14295, Gm11007, and Gm2007, although we also found genes such as Gsta1, an oxidative stress response gene that is one of the most differentially expressed between normal liver and steatotic liver (Hennig et al., 2014), and retinol metabolism genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b13, and Rdh9, which is part of a predictive signature for fibrosis in a mouse model for NASH (van Koppen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Koppen et al., 2018.

claim: Foxq1 is among the top downregulated genes in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Among the top downregulated genes, we identified Foxq1, an established repressor of FOXO1 (Cui et al., 2016), confirming the presence of insulin resistance in which FOXO1 is hyperactive.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citation to Cui et al., 2016.

claim: Foxq1 was expressed at normal levels in 8-week-old Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, Foxq1 was expressed at normal levels in the 8-week-old Cdk1 cKO mice (see Figure 1L), indicating that with age, there is an adaptive process regulating FOXQ1/FOXO1 activity.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from young mice (Figure 1L).

claim: With age, there is an adaptive process regulating FOXQ1/FOXO1 activity in Cdk1 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, Foxq1 was expressed at normal levels in the 8-week-old Cdk1 cKO mice (see Figure 1L), indicating that with age, there is an adaptive process regulating FOXQ1/FOXO1 activity.
evidence: Inferred from normal Foxq1 expression in young mice (Figure 1L) but downregulation in aged mice (RNA-seq).

claim: The severe NAFLD 20-gene signature is expressed substantially higher in aged Cdk1 cKO liver than in aged control liver.
source: When we compared the RNA-seq data to a 20-gene signature associated with severe NAFLD/NASH relative to mild NAFLD (Moylan et al., 2014), the gene signature appeared to be expressed substantially higher in aged Cdk1 cKO liver than in aged control liver (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and heat map (Figure 7C) with citation to Moylan et al., 2014.

claim: Selected genes from the severe NAFLD signature are upregulated in aged Cdk1 cKO liver as confirmed by qPCR.
source: We further validated selected targets within the gene signature via qPCR and confirmed that these genes were upregulated in aged Cdk1 cKO liver (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR validation data (Figure 7D).

claim: The 'retinol metabolism' pathway is the most significantly enriched pathway among upregulated genes in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 7) indicated a number of pathways are enriched among upregulated (red) and downregulated (green) genes from the RNA-seq. The most significantly enriched pathway, 'retinol metabolism', as well as enrichment of 'TGF-beta signaling pathway', provide support for the presence of fibrosis in Cdk1 cKO liver (Lee and Jeong, 2012; Meng et al., 2016) and confirmed our metabolomics data (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 7).

claim: Enrichment of 'TGF-beta signaling pathway' provides support for the presence of fibrosis in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 7) indicated a number of pathways are enriched among upregulated (red) and downregulated (green) genes from the RNA-seq. The most significantly enriched pathway, 'retinol metabolism', as well as enrichment of 'TGF-beta signaling pathway', provide support for the presence of fibrosis in Cdk1 cKO liver (Lee and Jeong, 2012; Meng et al., 2016) and confirmed our metabolomics data (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7E) and citations to Lee and Jeong, 2012 and Meng et al., 2016.

claim: Multiple KEGG terms associated with cancer are enriched for upregulated genes in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: Multiple KEGG terms associated with cancer, such as 'chemical carcinogenesis', 'cell cycle' and 'hepatocellular carcinoma' were also enriched for upregulated genes (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 7).

claim: The 'steroid hormone biosynthesis' pathway is enriched among downregulated genes in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
source: On the other hand, KEGG pathway analysis of downregulated genes only highlighted the term 'steroid hormone biosynthesis' (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 7).

claim: Downregulation of Hsd3b5 and Cyp2c70 is associated with development of NAFLD in mouse models.
source: Nevertheless, a closer inspection of genes classified under this term revealed Hsd3b5 and Cyp2c70 for which downregulation is associated with development of NAFLD in mouse models (Hou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hou et al., 2019.

claim: LXR is the most significant transcription factor identified by ChIP enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.
source: ChIP enrichment analysis (ChEA) was also performed on the transcriptomic data to identify transcription factors whose downstream targets are enriched among differentially expressed genes (Figure 7F, Supplementary file 7). LXR, a glucose-responsive lipogenic nuclear receptor (Mitro et al., 2007), was the most significant transcription factor identified.
evidence: Supported by ChEA analysis of RNA-seq data (Figure 7F, Supplementary file 7).

claim: LXR is a glucose-responsive lipogenic nuclear receptor.
source: ChIP enrichment analysis (ChEA) was also performed on the transcriptomic data to identify transcription factors whose downstream targets are enriched among differentially expressed genes (Figure 7F, Supplementary file 7). LXR, a glucose-responsive lipogenic nuclear receptor (Mitro et al., 2007), was the most significant transcription factor identified.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitro et al., 2007.

claim: LXR binds to DNA as a heterodimer with RXR.
source: LXR binds to DNA as a heterodimer with RXR (Willy et al., 1995), which also appears as an enriched transcription factor, indicating that the LXR-RXR heterodimer may be more active in the aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
evidence: Supported by citation to Willy et al., 1995.

claim: The LXR-RXR heterodimer may be more active in aged Cdk1 cKO liver.
